utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Monday, the 2nd of March, 2009. Good afternoon to Mr. Stojic, Mr. Praljak, and Mr. Pusic. And good afternoon to all the Defence counsel and all the OTP representatives, as well as all the people assisting us. And Mr. Registrar, you have a few IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. Some parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Kvesic, Ante. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC 00933, and the list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC 00934. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Trial Chamber is going to issue a short ruling regarding rules as regards filing of exhibits submitted to witnesses in testimony. The Trial Chamber noted that lately the parties have filed their requests for admission through written filings and not through IC lists. The Trial Chamber recalls that such requests have to comply with the procedure as per paragraph 32 of the decision on the adoption of guide-lines for Defence exhibits, of the 24th of April, 2008, and this cannot be changed with the procedure for filing motions in writing. So, in other words, you have to use the IC procedure in order to seek to admit exhibits. We are going to have a new witness. He's a protected witness. Mr. Usher, make sure that the blinds are lowered so that the witness can enter the courtroom, and we're going to move to closed session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's go back to the beginning of May 1992. What happened then? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already said that (redacted) 13 (redacted) 14 (redacted) 15 (redacted) 16 (redacted) But I also had to do all the jobs that my colleagues did, so I had to go to the front-line, and a team came from the Main Medical Corps' headquarters, Dr. Kolak, Bagaric, and Kvesic from Siroki Brijeg, and Dr. Kolak told me that if I wanted to and if there was the opportunity, that I could move to the Main Medical Corps centre in view of the fact that at the time and in that territory there were no doctors who were well versed in preventive medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you talk about the front-line and the period that we're talking about - we're now talking about April and May - just for the transcript, can you tell us what was happening at that time, whether the war had started, whether there were conflicts, and if so, which units were involved, and which units were you part of, who were they fighting against, and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were members of the Croatian Defence Council who, together with the Muslim armed forces, fought a war against the aggressors; specifically, the Serb Army and the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we heard that you were given this offer of transferring to the area of preventive medicine to the Main Medical Corps headquarters. Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They called me soon after that, so, yes, that's right. I was called to go to Tomislavgrad, where I came into contact with the deputy of the head of the Main Medical Corps headquarters, Dr. Salic and Dr. Kolak, since Dr. Bagaric was not at the meeting. And on that occasion, we looked at what could be done, how to use -- how best to use my knowledge and my experience. And I'd like to repeat that we had very few doctors, as we do today, in the field of preventive medicine, and so I was offered this job because, as an infectologist or specialist in infectious diseases, it was a close area of medicine. And in the former army where I worked, preventive medicine was considered to be a very important part of the work done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said epidemiology, you said epidemiology was a very important sector, so when you use these medical terms, could you say them slowly so they could be properly recorded. So do you accept -- did you accept this offer, and did you, in fact, become a member of the Main Medical Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How? Tell us in what way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, my assignments were defined, my tasks and duties were defined, and among other things it was said that I would be number-one man in the area of preventive medicine and that it was my duty, for the area covered by the HZ-HB, to set up teams to educate the population in the field of preventive medicine and the rules governing that area, and I'm going to talk about preventive medicine and protection, that field. And it was also my duty to send regular reports so that my superiors, and I'm using military language there, so that my superiors could be kept abreast of the hygiene, epidemiological situation, both in settled -- in built-up areas and in the army and on the battle-fields. And because we lacked cadres among the civilian structures, it was up to me to integrate all these functions, so not only to do work for the HVO but to cater to the civilian population as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you receive a decision of any kind telling you to form this service for preventive medicine, and if so, when, and who signed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I received a decision to that effect signed by Dr. Sarac, that is to say, the deputy to our head, to our chief, and that was on the 9th of May, 1992, and in that -- that decision sets out all my tasks and responsibilities, with a final point stating that I should always prioritise and determine what the priorities were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you received this decision on the 9th of May, 1992, as you said, there was the Main Medical Corps headquarters with its seat in Tomislavgrad; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, after you received that decision, where did you set up, where was your headquarters, where was your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pursuant to permission from Dr. Sarac and Dr. Kolak, I went to Siroki Brijeg, and the reason being was that I knew all my colleagues there because, as a specialist, I was a well-known doctor in the region, and I thought that it was easier for me to start working from there, from an environment that I knew, and to set up a team there, because there was nothing. We had to start from scratch, set up a team from scratch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you had to start from scratch, as you've just told us, you weren't a specialist in preventive medicine either, but if we look at Herzegovina as a whole, were there enough doctors and staff who, in any way, either as doctors, nurses, or staff of that kind, who knew what was to be done in the field of prevention or was there a deficiencies of cadres there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a deficit of staff, and rationalisation had to be put in place. I had to rationalise with the men -- with the people available. And today, for example, in peacetime, there is a deficit in people trained in the preventive health area. And in the world, public health is a highly respected area, but in primitive environments such as my own, it is considered an area of lesser importance and that there's a negative selection of physicians that are not as highly trained. But let me go back to the period we're discussing. There weren't enough people working in that field, and so epidemiology was perhaps the closest area, and I don't think that at that time you would have found a better man than myself for the job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said that your task was to establish teams. Could you please tell the Honourable Trial Chamber whether you did set up these teams, and how and where they existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already said, I had this integrative function because there weren't enough trained people, so first of all in Siroki Brijeg I had to establish that, which was a test for me as to whether I'd be successful in other areas. Thankfully, I had this idea that a team had to consist of people whose knowledge, dedication, and efforts could prevent the outbreak of infectious diseases, so I set up a team in Siroki Brijeg, and the same kinds of teams were set up elsewhere. I'm going to repeat that, because I think it's very important. The teams had the same composition everywhere. There was a physician who was head of the team. Then there was a vet who was in charge of food that was animal or, rather, non-vegetarian food. Then we also had another person who hopefully had worked in the sanitary inspectorate before that, and then also there'd had to be a driver in the team. When I set up the team in Siroki Brijeg, I sent reports straight away to Tomislavgrad, to the Main Medical Corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the transcript, you said that there was a doctor, a physician, who was head of the team, a vet, an agronomist and a driver; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And somebody who had worked for the sanitary inspectorate before the war as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me one follow-up question. We understand that you set up this structure for infectious diseases, but I have a question. Back in the former Yugoslavia, if somebody had a serious disease, would that person be sent to Belgrade, to Sarajevo, or to Zagreb, or was that person treated on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, infectious diseases are a specific matter. These are contagious diseases. They can be transferred from one person to another, but then also from an animal to a person. Then infectious or contagious diseases can also cause an epidemic. And you also know that there can be a pandemic too. In Mostar, we had a department for infectious diseases, and that is where patients were sent, patients with such diseases. (redacted) (redacted)-- or, rather, that at that time we sent very, very few patients to Belgrade and Zagreb for further treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's be more specific. Let us imagine -- but of course there was no risk at all at the time, but let us imagine there was this avian flu in 1992. Would that person have been treated in Mostar or would you have sent that patient to Belgrade, Sarajevo, or Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're talking about 1992, up until May probably we would have provided treatment in Mostar, and then after May, I don't know exactly what date it was when the roads were cut off, then we would treat them in Mostar, but we would send more difficult cases to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His Honour asked you about this network, and the network that you're talking about was a network for preventive medicine; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, preventive medicine. Perhaps you didn't hear me right. I do apologise. Because there weren't enough people around, so then I had people who were dealing with curative medicine before that, and then I transferred them to work with -- work in the field of preventive medicine. As the English would say, this is variegated medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it -- what was it that you said in English, that it was a big difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, an enormous difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You established these teams in order to prevent contagious diseases; right? You explained why, and how, and what the principle was, and who you had on these teams. We are done with Siroki Brijeg, so could you tell us briefly where it was that you established these teams further on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Siroki Brijeg was just the first station that we had, an experimental one at that, and then I realised that I would be successful. Then there was a meeting in Capljina that was attended by representatives of municipalities, that is to say, doctors, medical people from Neum, Capljina, Citluk and Ljubusko. And then in every one of these towns, we established respective teams - I don't have to repeat it - consisting of the same profile of experts. Then I went to Grude, where yet again doctors from Grude and Posusje met, and what was established was a team, again of the same composition in those towns. After that, I went to Livno, which is a major centre, where yet again a team was established with the same composition, that is to say, for carrying out these functions in the field of preventive medicine. Then I went to Jablanica, where yet again a team was established. However, this time for Konjic, Jablanica. And since there were colleagues there from Central Bosnia, Mr. Djambas, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Teams were set up, so I made up these teams pretty well, and I covered the entire territory. Perhaps I can also add that this package of measures was introduced in Posavina as well. However, I was not in charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, now that we are discussing all these teams, were civilian and military personnel on these teams, and was their role to contain contagious diseases, both in places where civilians lived or in the civilian sector, if we can put it that way, and in the military sector?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've already said there were very few such people around, and I've already said that contagious diseases did not make a distinction between civilians and military personnel, it is simply human beings that are affected. So if you prevent contagious diseases in an area, then you're dealing with the entire population of that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not answer my question. Who were members of this team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I tend to wander off. They were civilians, for the most part, persons who worked in civilian structures. So in that way, in view of the profile of these people who were trained, who had an education, we managed to cover the entire territory of that municipality, both the civilian and military segments. However, I've already said our function was an integrative one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you establish any other team that was attached to the Main Medical Corps headquarters? Did you establish that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In order for this to work, a professional, educational, instructive body had to be established that had to help those teams at that given point in time. That is why I established a team attached to the Main Medical Corps headquarters, not to repeat it, a physician, a vet and so on. It was called a mobile team, a mobile team. As this is self-explanatory, it is a mobile team and they are supposed to go where their assistance is required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, all of these teams that you established in this area, I'm asking you about 1992, 1993 and, say, April 1994. Throughout this time, did they cover these areas for which they were in charge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about you and your mobile team; did you go from time to time to these areas where these teams that were in charge of these areas were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was our task. We went to see how they worked, to resolve problems, and also every time I went somewhere, that was a good opportunity to instruct people, to train them. The domicile teams were professionally stronger after every one of my visits, and there are reports to support that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for reports, these teams from the other areas and your team, your mobile team, who was it that you actually submitted these reports to about hygienic and epidemiological examinations that you carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I forgot to say that all teams worked in the same composition. I tried to introduce something that exists in all armies of the world, and that is a single medical military doctrine, in terms of preventive medicine. I would like to underline that. So all my work was focused on preventive medical protection, and all teams worked on that in Grude, Posusje, and this main team worked on the basis of the same principle. And now, as far as your question is concerned, the reports, we would send them to where we had come from. If it's the civilian sector, then we'd send it to the civilian authority involved and also, of course, to the Main Medical Corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also go on such missions to military units, and then who would you report to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, we were established, inter alia, to practice preventive medicine in the HVO. After every examination, there would have to be a report. But I would like to point out that each and every time, I was accompanied by the main person from the medical unit of that particular unit, and he would familiarise himself with the preventive medicine situation in that unit. And then if we were lucky, we would go to the commander of the unit, and then the same day, usually in the evening, I would write a report to that unit, and I'd send a report usually to the superior unit, and also to the Main Medical Corps headquarters, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as you were doing all of this work in an identical way, did you work in this way on the basis of this identical model throughout your tour of duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've said that from the moment I started working and up until the very end of my tour of duty, I worked in the field of preventive medicine, and on the basis of this model of a single military medical doctrine. I was engaged up until the end of 1995 in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as far as units are concerned, I would like to remind you, and also for the purpose of the transcript, we are still dealing with 1992. We haven't even come to June, so I'm asking about that period, and then we'll deal with the other period of time. You said that you had contact with the head of the medical units within the larger units. You had such contacts. Did you have them in the same way later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in terms of the units involved, who were the persons that you had contacted, persons who were, in a way, in charge of the medical needs of that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since most of these units were at brigade level, that is to say, tactical groups, I had contacts with the head of the medical service of that brigade, and then I would communicate with that head or chief, and then I'd go down to lower-ranking units, like battalions and even companies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professionally, what was the professional background of this chief medical officer of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was supposed to be a physician, a general practitioner; that is to say, not a specialist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about companies and battalions; did they have medical personnel with some kind of medical qualifications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we start with the lowest level, that's company level, that would be a nurse. In my country, there used to be a school for nursing, and then it no longer existed. Most of them came from the former Yugoslav People's Army. They were people who underwent such training, but were not professional nurses. They knew very little. They could give first aid and provide very basic medical protection. Several companies comprised a battalion. At the battalion level, there would be a medical technician, of course, with the proper degree of training, of course, with a higher level of medical knowledge both in the field of preventive medicine and also in terms of providing care, and then there would be a few orderlies to help him out. If necessary, if there was combat involved, then he'd send them to lower-ranking units, too. Then several battalions comprise a brigade, and then there were military districts further up, and then there would be heads of the medical service for the entire military district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as for your own line of work that we've been discussing so far, that is to say, prevention, preventing sources of infection and disease, in which way did you have professional contacts with these persons who were in charge of medical affairs in different units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I would establish contact with such a person. I would go to the unit involved. I would talk to my colleague. I would say to him what it was that he was supposed to do. I would like to point out that I have written several handbooks and several sets of instructions. You must realise that these were young people, people who did not have sufficient knowledge, people with big hearts, but at that point in time they had very little knowledge. I was supposed to educate them in terms of preventive medical care, and I underline that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you their superior? Your service that was involved with preventive medical care, was it in a superior position in relation to them? What was the relationship between your service and these persons in different units that were in charge of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not take part in the chain of command, because the medical corps in all armies throughout the world is a professional body, engaged in training as well, which makes proposals, and if you looked at the many, many reports that I wrote, I always propose measures. Now, as far as the professional area goes, we were professionally superior to them, that's true, and it was our duty to train them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you to tell the Trial Chamber now what happened in around June and July with the Main Medical Corps HQ. Did it dislocate from Tomislavgrad, did it move?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Mostar was liberated at that time, and I was given the task of going to Mostar to be one of the main people to pave the way for the Main Medical Corps HQ to relocate and to set up a mobile team as well, so that I had in fact two mobile teams as of that date. And until the arrival of a Main Medical Corps HQ, I was placed at the disposal of the war hospital in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, where you were accommodated when you reached Mostar, and when the Main Medical Corps HQ arrived, where was that put up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostar itself was very much devastated at the time. It was destroyed. And at the beginning of the war, the Main Medical Corps HQ was in the building where the Defence Department worked; that is, later on, of course. After that, we relocated to another public facility a kilometre and a half away, which is the new hospital where, before the war, small sections of it were working. But during the war, it stopped working, and so we took over some offices on the ground floor, and that's where the Main Medical Corps HQ was relocated to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, Witness. You are translated and recorded here as saying the following: "At the beginning of the war, the Main Medical Corps was in the building where the Defence Department worked; that is, later on, of course." This reads contradictory, and I would be grateful if you could clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my mistake. The Main Medical Corps headquarters was in Tomislavgrad. However, with the liberation of Mostar from the Serb aggression, it was relocated to Mostar, so that -- we're talking about June and July here. Now, at that point, for a very short period of time we were in a building of the former Tobacco Institute. That's a building where later on -- later on the Defence Department came into being. So after spending a short time there, we went to the hospital at Bijeli Brijeg which was under construction and has actually just been completed quite recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we're talking about June 1992. That's what you're talking about, Witness; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned the hospital at Bijeli Brijeg. Now, as we had a witness in court here last week, I'd like to ask you to explain to the Trial Chamber -- well, we had Dr. Ante Kvesic, that was the witness, and he was the head of the war hospital, so could you explain to Their Honours where that particular war hospital was located or explain to us whether those were two hospitals that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is two hospitals, and these two hospitals are about three to four kilometres apart from each other. My colleague, Dr. Kvesic, was the head of the hospital, but he was in the hospital that was up at the front-line, and many world magazines and journals wrote about that. This other hospital was under construction, and as I say, it is three or four kilometres away from the first one. They are physically separated and have nothing in common. But Dr. Kvesic was the head doctor, the manager of that first hospital, but they are -- we're talking about two completely different hospitals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, after the Main Medical Corps HQ relocated in 1992, and I'm asking you about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, please, I'm trying to understand. You said that Dr. Kvesic was in the hospital that was on the front-line. I'm a little bit puzzled, therefore. When you say that it was on the front-line, does this mean that this was a hospital that took charge of those people that had been wounded during the war, that's why this hospital was on the front-line? Was that the reason why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mostar -- the whole of Mostar, the town was the front-line, in fact, and this hospital was at a forward post, it was exposed, and it functioned until very recently, the surgery ward. But, anyway, that's the hospital in town, whereas this other hospital is -- the new hospital that I'm talking about is along the periphery, the outskirts of town, if I can put it that way. So they're two completely different localities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take the case of a wounded HVO soldier. The soldier is wounded. Which hospital is he taken to, the one that's on the front-line, or is this person taken to your hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first hospital that Dr. Kvesic spoke about. It was operational before the war as well, but the other hospital started working in mid-July 1993, so there's just this discontinuity in time. To begin with, only one hospital was working. Later on, both of them functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's take the case of an HVO soldier. In August of 1993, he receives a bullet in his chest. Which hospital is he taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would take them where there was available space; mostly to the first hospital. But as there are a lot of wounded persons, then they would be evacuated to the upper hospital, that is to say, the other hospital as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A second case, let's take the case of a child that coughs relentless -- unrelentlessly, that spits out blood. Which hospital is this child taken to, the first hospital or the second?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A child coughing will go to the pediatric department which was up on the hill very close to the new hospital, because pediatrics, as you know, is a branch of medicine dealing with children's diseases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But let me just ask you, Witness: The second hospital, where you say was where the Main Medical Corps HQ was located, you talked about that during the Naletilic/Martinovic trial, and that's why I wanted us to differentiate an distinguish between the hospitals, but I think it's very important at this point for you to explain to Their Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I'd like the interpreter in the French booth to do his or her job. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it's important for you to explain to the Trial Chamber whether the hospital, that second hospital where the Main Medical Corps HQ was located, had it been completed before the war? Why wasn't it working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hospital has just been opened just a few days ago, and I can say with pride that it is a specialised hospital, and my boss, Dr. Ante Kvesic, whom you saw, has been proclaimed one of the main citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But before that, only a small portion had been constructed, but the hospital was finished just a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, we've cleared that up now. Now, you said in September/October 1992 -- or tell me, whether during that time there was some reorganisation that took place, and where was the Main Medical Corps HQ put up, and did you remain in the same locality you were in before this reorganisation took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in August, there was reorganisation, so we were no longer referred to as the Main Medical Corps HQ, but we became the Sector for Health attached to the Defence Department, and the Health Sector had three parts. One was the Main Medical Corps, so it stayed within that sector. The second sector was for the wounded, and the third sector was for inspection and control. I was in the Main Medical Corps, and above me -- well, when I say "I," that might not be the right way to put it. I might be accused of boasting. But there was a team -- there was a team for dentistry, for informatics, for storage, and Mr. Kvesic was our head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, so with the establishment of the Defence document, one of its sectors was the Health Sector, as you said, and it was within this sector, the Health Sector, that your service was located within the Main Medical Corps HQ; is that right? Have I interpreted that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, you said you received your first decision, signed by Mr. Sarac, as you explained to us, but later on, up to 1995, as you said, did these decisions change? Did you receive any other decisions from other individuals, and did your tasks and assignments change and the job you did, did that change too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have already said that from the time I started working in the Main Medical Corps HQ, until I finished working within the HVO, I always did the same job, my duties were all the same, always in the sphere of preventive medicine. Now, as far as decisions are concerned, one was for Dr. Bagaric, one from -- was from Mr. Perica Jukic, the minister, and one was from Mr. Vlado Soljic, but only in the field of preventive medicine. Let me stress that once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Nozica, soon the first hour of the hearing of this witness is over. I must confess to you that I have not found anything that links anywhere to the indictment. You will say this -- probably that this belongs to joint criminal enterprise, because that's what you always say in the Defence, but I don't see how it does. It would be interesting for the medical history of Mostar, but that is not what we are exactly dealing with. Could you try to concentrate a bit and put questions and solicit answers which assist the Bench in its task. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that these are very significant issues, and I'm not going to say that it's important for the joint criminal enterprise, but to come to the merits of the case and the merits of the indictment, we have to explain the genesis of everything. I know how much time I have at my disposal, so I can assure you that this basic information will be very important for you to understand what comes later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you came to Mostar in 1992, tell us briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, one moment, please. I agree entirely with what my colleague Judge Trechsel has just said. We've just spent an hour listening to you, and I'm very expectant. I don't know what the latter half of your questions will focus on. I don't see in what way they are assisting us. Maybe you want to create a degree of suspense, but we are waiting impatiently for these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... become quite clear in just a moment, but let's bear in mind the indictment, and the Health Sector within the indictment, and the position of the service in which this witness was working, for us to be able to explain what his task was. We have to put it in the general context, the overall tasks responsibilities of this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, since Their Honours are impatient to hear the crux of the matter, the substance of the issues, could you explain to them just briefly how, when you arrived in Mostar in 1992, onwards -- or, rather, what your main tasks were. What areas did you have to visit in order to prevent the outbreak of diseases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already said, the team's function was integral, to look at the military and civilian sector, and according to the postulates of epidemiology, was to visit the waterworks system. Secondly, to visit everywhere where people congregated in large numbers, because if you have large numbers, there's always the danger of infectious and contagious diseases which could become epidemics. Third, to visit food supplies and the utilities companies. Then, number 5, to go with the units. I had to come into contact with all persons concerned and everybody who could help me prevent the outbreak of infectious diseases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the waterworks system, you mentioned civilian institutions and locations, you mentioned visiting the units. Could you explain to Their Honours, who did you talk to when you went to visit the waterworks system, for example, and who did you send a report to, reporting on the conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The waterworks are a central location. I went to the director, to the manager, and I always demanded that a residual chlorine be at a level 0.3 to 0.4, and then I would send out a report to the civilian authorities and to the Health Sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when it comes to water and Mostar, are there any specific features to be noted in that year of 1992? What was specific with water then? Did Mostar have sufficient water supplies? I'm talking about 1992 and especially 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1993 -- or, rather, 1993 was -- has been described as Mostar's driest year. Now, Mostar had two waterworks systems, and the amount of water -- because of the amount of shelling, many of the pipes had been damaged, and the water levels ran very low, and there was the permanent danger of water contamination from the sewage system, which would lead to an outbreak of intestinal diseases. Now, I lived in town, in the center of town. I was on the fifth floor of a high-rise building, and I didn't have any water, so we had to go down to the hydrant and take water there for the basics, the essentials.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see, thank you. Now, could you explain to the Trial Chamber, what of your tours to the units? What did you do when you went to tour a unit, who did you talk to, and what were your priorities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you answer Ms. Nozica's question, let me go back to the issue of water. I now discover that you were living in the center of Mostar, that you did not get any water, and that you had to go to the hydrant to get some water. As far as you know, was there anyone in Mostar who died of thirst or who died because they did not have enough water or who suffered serious consequences because they could not drink any water? Was there a single case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot say with any degree of certainty. I mean, I don't know. That's what I'm saying, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: While we're at it in the same vein, Witness. Can you tell us about any epidemics that broke out during the war in Mostar due to unclean water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not in Mostar, nowhere at the level of Herceg-Bosna was there a single epidemic, not through water, not through food, and I personally consider that to be the achievement of my life, and I -- [In English] [Indiscernible] is a world famous medical journal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I did not have the translation, but the last words were in English, I can see. I can only say congratulations. I'm still waiting for a link to the indictment, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you don't see that in the case of water, in the case of water in Mostar, then perhaps I don't understand what would be significant in terms of this witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we are going to go back to the question of water in Mostar, as you've said that was the water situation in Mostar, in the west part of Mostar in 1993. However, there is a report about that, and that's a very important topic. For the transcript, I would just like to say that the witness revealed his identity on lines 13 and 14 on page 14, so I don't think it would be a bad idea to have that section redacted. Now, Witness, very briefly, very concisely, could you explain to the Honourable Trial Chamber about this mobile team of yours when you went to work on prevention in a particular unit? Could you explain who you met up with and where you carried out examinations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, we would go to the chief medical officer of that unit, say in a brigade, say in Capljina was Dr. Sutalo. First of all, we would talk and see whether there were any problems. Yet again, I'm saying in the field of preventive medical care. Are there any contagious diseases there? Are there any individual cases of this nature, is there a link between and among them, and whether there is a possibility of an epidemic breaking out. I would like to note that water is very important. I'll just give you the example of the city of Hamburg in 1812. 2.600 people got cholera. In cholera -- in Pristina, over 1.000 people got cholera. Take cholera -- or, rather, typhoid, and cholera is a very important -- that's a very important case. There was a lot of cholera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, there is no need for you to lapse into English, because you can just confuse the interpreters by speaking both languages at the same time. Just tell us what you focused on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, water. We had to -- we had to find how much residual chlorine there was. That is to say, if there was no residual chlorine in water, then that water should not be imbibed. It is potentially dangerous because it has microbiological agents. We carried out such checks in respect of food, too, because food can also lead to infections. We know that today, even in big hotel chains like Hilton, say there was an outbreak of salmonella in Glasgow five years ago, and so on and so forth. Also, we looked at what accommodation was for the soldiers, I mean, that we have to make a distinction between barracks and front-lines, but I guess we'll be dealing with that later. Also, we looked at what waste disposal was like. You know full well that if that is inadequate, then that is one of the possible vectors that lead to the outbreak of contagious diseases. Further on, I looked at what the medical supplies were, from the point of view of preventive medicine. Also, I asked to see medical documentation. Unfortunately, at first there wasn't any; later on, there were medical documents, because adequate medical documentation could reflect what the health situation was. I will say for a hundred times, if necessary, that every time I educated and trained my colleagues, we had people who had university degrees, who had knowledge, but no experience, and I would like to say that public health had totally been neglected in my country, regrettably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, what you say about West Mostar -- or based on what you said, everything was done, but our problem is about East Mostar. So what did you do for East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no one asked me. As soon as I arrived in Mostar, I established contact with my colleagues from the left bank. Also, I carried out this education that I'm so proud of. I'm digressing now, but two months ago there was an epidemic of infectious hepatitis on the left bank among some refugees. I was called by these people, and I prevented an epidemic; that is to say, that I had this educational role to play, and I'm very proud of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that you were in touch with your colleagues in East Mostar and that, together with them, you would monitor the health or sanitary conditions regarding water and food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour, yes (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we need to redact this line, because knowing your colleagues name, you would be identified easily. We're going to have an order. Mr. Registrar, please prepare it. Continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a small question. The yellow fever, I think it was, epidemic that you spoke about a moment ago, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it wasn't yellow fever, it was virus Hepatitis A, so that was very important. It broke out just now. I am an infectologist, but they called me even now, and I'm very proud of that. I was on federal TV and talked about it for an hour. Yellow fever, that is a disease --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It was a linguistic problem, because Hepatitis B in Germany is called "Gelbsucht," as you may know, and "gelb" is yellow, so I mixed it up. I'm sorry, you're quite right. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Wir konnen aber Deutsch sprechen, wenn Sie wollen mochten. Es ist mir ganz egal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But we are not here for a dialogue, Doctor, unfortunately. This is for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you haven't been asked, but I do intend to ask you. However, His Honour Judge Antonetti asked first. When you said that you carried out this education of your colleagues on the east bank, can you explain when it was that this had happened? Was it before the conflict between the Bosniaks and Croats? And tell me, in terms of this education, did you also go to locations where the units were, the then units, say, of the Mostar Battalion? Later on, these were units of the 4th Corps. Did you visit these localities in an identical fashion, as you had been doing in the case of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need a redaction of line 13, page 35, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I carried out this education. The system of work for me was absolutely identical, regardless of whether it had to do with the right bank or the left bank, regardless of whether it had to do with civilians or the military. It was based on the single military medical doctrine. In response to your question, yes, yes, I went to the front-line of the BH Army and the HVO. The same education went to all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a technical question for you, based on what you said just now. We have heard a lot of witnesses. We've been sitting here for over two years. We've heard a lot of witnesses, and I remember a woman. She was going to fetch some water from the river, and she was killed by sniper fire. I'd like to know this: Somebody getting water from the stream, could they boil the water in order to drink it afterwards, without putting any chlorine in it? Can it be drunk then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. First of all, you said "the river." It must be the Neretva. I assume that it was a conflict between the two warring parties. Water can be boiled and even used for disinfection later on. So, yes, I often did that myself. I often took such water myself. And it is a crime to kill anyone anywhere at any time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you said just now how you toured this unit. Tell me very briefly, because time is short, after touring the headquarters of the unit, did you go to the front-line too or, rather, out into the field where the troops were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was a real doctor, not a salon doctor. I did go, indeed, not only in the case of the HVO, but also the BH Army, and I'm so proud of that, very proud of that, and everyone knows that from all structures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, after that, after all these tours, did you compile a report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you submitted them according to the methodology that you already described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, now I'm going to put a few questions to you about conditions on the front in respect of the HVO units. We are talking about the period after the conflict with the BH Army. I would be interested in three segments. Since you often went to the front-line, I would be interested in hearing about three segments. Where were the soldiers sleeping? What kind of food did they have, and what kind of water did they have? Can you briefly explain to the Trial Chamber what your experience is in relation to these three conditions under which HVO members lived at the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, you asked about sleep. As for sleep, at the front-line two elements have to be distinguished. One group of soldiers would be at the front-line and others would be resting. They would be resting mostly in houses that were heavily damaged, often had no water, and often they even used tents. I would like to say that the same goes for the Muslim forces too. As for food, food came from the central kitchen of that particular unit. However, the basic postulate was that if food is consumed, two hours after it is cooked, it should not be used. We have to realise there were soldiers who were at forward posts, and they only ate dry food, not cooked meals. And what was your third question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Water.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was very little water. I think that it was only sufficient to meet the basic needs of organisms; 0.3 or 0.4 per cent was the allowed percentage of chlorine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as sleep is concerned, according to your experience, you toured all these units, these houses where they were, did they have beds? We're talking about abandoned houses. You said that primarily they were in these houses that had been abandoned. Did they have blankets, and what was the situation like in the very beginning, and did it improve somewhat as time went by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There weren't any beds. They slept on spreads, and they had blankets. I personally wrote and asked for these blankets to be washed and disinfected. Unfortunately, that is one of the segments that no one took care of. At first, they thought that my requests were impossible, and they thought that I brought that from the former army. They did not realise that this was prevention of skin diseases. And I also need to point out that at first, due to indolence and ignorance, they didn't want to dig toilets either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Food. What was your assessment? If it was brought from food -- from the brigade, was there enough food, was the quality good? What would your general assessment of the food be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In all armies of the world, there is this system of cooking large quantities of food at the same time and also that cannot get infected easily, so throughout the world food does not vary to a great deal. It is insufficiently varied. At first, it wasn't very good, but later on it got better. There wasn't enough variety. The quality was fairly good, but due to epidemiological reasons, they had to make due.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The members of the HVO, of the Croatian Defence Council, as far as water is concerned, in this situation when they were at the front-line, did they have enough water for hygiene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was very little water. There was just enough to keep them alive from a biological point of view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, now that we have painted this general picture, could you please respond to the Trial Chamber and say whether you went to prisons, isolation locations, or centres where prisoners of war were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall when it was that you first visited a locality called a prison or that was in one of the mentioned categories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look, I've already said, but you may have forgotten, every large group of people, if they are at the same locality, they provide fertile ground for the outbreak of infectious diseases. In winter months, it is respiratory diseases; throughout the year, stomach-related diseases and also nervous disorders, including even meningitis. For me, a prison is a house where people are kept and are not allowed to leave. From a medical point of view, that's it. I went for the first time when my colleague, (redacted), asked me -- or, rather, I have to tell you something else before that. I came from the former army. (redacted) had very good relations. However, I realised that if -- if someone who is my superior said something to me, that was an order for me, although it was not an order, necessarily. That was my understanding of the matter. I went to the spot itself. I went there to do my work, and my colleague, (redacted), said to me, It seems that at the Heliodrom, there are many people who had been assembled there. Please go and see what this is all about. Please take care of it all, from the point of view of preventive medicine. Please don't allow anything inappropriate to happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, "Don't allow any epidemiological incident to take place." Was that the end of your sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tend to sometimes swallow your words, so that wasn't recorded. Can you tell me when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was in mid-May 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you go to prisons that were called Dretelj and Gabela?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do that in the same way -- did (redacted) tell you or did you learn that those prisons had been formed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think my colleague (redacted), but the way in which I worked was -- well, 85 per cent of the decisions I took myself. However, when you're engaged in preventive medicine, you have to go on location. You're not a doctor in a hospital. You have to go on location and take measures to prevent diseases, so that is your vocation, to go on the spot, on location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we move on to the documents that tell us about that, let's clear up a few points. Witness, you, as a doctor, and I'm asking you this because of the questions you were asked during the Naletilic/Martinovic trial, did you differentiate between prisons, detention centres, detention and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the difference now and I didn't know the difference then. As far as I'm concerned, it's all the same, all one thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We have just a little time left before the break. Can you explain to us, when you toured these places and localities, was the system of work in force for the control of these premises identical as you explained to us earlier on, the system you applied when you went to the units, whether it was HVO units or previously the BH Army units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, yes, I did -- I worked according to a uniform medical doctrine for wartime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the priorities, could you repeat that, in all these places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the same thing would happen if I went to see refugees. I didn't make any differentiation between refugees, displaced persons, soldiers and the prisons. The priorities were, let me repeat, water, food, accommodation, dealing with waste matter, and then whether documents were being kept, whether the right documents were being sent out, and, furthermore, the education and training of the population, whether they be doctors or whoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are now addressing an essential issue. You said that you would go and visit these people, refugees, military, or prisoners. I'm quoting there. I want to know the following: When you would go to the Heliodrom, would you go and see free people, or people who were detained, or still people having another status? Or you, as a doctor of medicine, you didn't ask yourself that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as a physician, and now as an assistant professor, as far as I'm concerned, I have taken the Hippocratic oath, so as far as I'm concerned, there are no prefixes that I apply. A man is a man, regardless of his title. All I distinguish between is healthy and sick, young/old, male/female. I know of no other categories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the time has come for a break. We're going to break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Ms. Nozica, you have had 58 minutes so far. You have one hour and two minutes. Therefore, I would like to mention to the witness that he should avoid mentioning names of people, because when that happens, this may identify you. When you have a question, raise your hand, and then we shall move into closed session. Otherwise, I will spend my afternoon signing redaction orders. I have three already, and I'm waiting for the Registrar to hand me a pen. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the Judge has just told you what I wanted to tell you, because the problem throughout your testimony was the fact that you mention names. Now, we have the transcript of your testimony during the Naletilic trial, and during that testimony you enjoyed the same protective measures, and the same names were mentioned then that you mention now. Now, if you want to name names, then ask us to go into closed session so that we don't have to redact the transcript. I know that Dr. Bagaric and all the other names were mentioned many times, and you had no problem there, but if you have a problem with names, then you let us know in advance and we'll move into private session. Anyway, let's move on. My last questions were related to the visits to the prisons, detention centres, and so on. We mentioned Heliodrom, Dretelj, Gabela. Now, as far as that portion of your testimony is concerned, tell us, please, who you went to tour these places with, and we'll move on to the documents afterwards. Who took you to those prisons? Who did you go there with? Who did you report to? Who did you go with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that I came with my -- one of my fellow workers to the unit, and if you looked at the reports, it always says that one of my staff was with me. Secondly, I reported to the chief of the medical corps of the said unit. If I was in Capljina, specifically, then I would report to the chief of the Knez Domagoj Medical Corps. If I was in the area of the 3rd Brigade, I would talk to their commander. And I would discuss the situation in the unit first, we would analyse the situation in the unit, and let me emphasise all this concerning preventive medicine and what measures to take in that regard. Then, we would take a look at the infirmary and the medicines to see whether there was sufficient supplies of medicines, and I asked every time to see all the medical documentation, and on that basis I was able to see the death rate, if there had been, or I could -- was able to conclude whether any infectious diseases had occurred. Now, after that, I would ask the chiefs, the commanders, whether there was anything they had failed to inform me of. And I would always ask, when I went to prisons, what the situation there was, and they would describe the situation. And once the head person had done that, then the two of us would go and tour the said locality. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll go into all the details and look at your reports, but I just want to ask you: Who was in charge of dealing with the medical care and attention of persons in these prisons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you read my reports and some of the instructions that were issued by the Health Sector, it was the unit that was there that was superior. So if we're talking about Capljina, the medical corps of the Knez Domagoj Brigade. If it was Mostar, Heliodrom. Then the chief of the medical corps would be the chief of the 3rd Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we look at the documents, tell me whether you used the same methods and methodology, as you explained to us earlier on, whenever you visited these places and compiled your reports, and tell us how you structured your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All my reports were done in a uniform manner, based on a uniform wartime medical doctrine, and the same system applied, and I worked with refugees, with army members, and in the prisons as well. The structure of the report was as follows: Well, I would state my views orally first and then write all this down and say there was water, which was extremely important from the aspects of medical prevention. Then we would look at accommodation. After that, we would look to see whether there were any specific diseases. I would examine persons myself. Then residues, waste matter, how that was seen to, where the persons were accommodated, what they had to cover themselves with, and so on. I've already mentioned waste matter and so on. And then on the basis of all these factors, I would compile a report. And if we are dealing with a prison, for example, if that's what you meant, then I would get information from the brigade physician, Dr. Hadzic or the late Dr. Stranjak, but also I would talk to people myself and ask people I knew personally, so that my report was always compiled in a multi-disciplinary approach to the problems in hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you give me shorter answers. I asked you about the structure. Did you first of all note down who was present? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all the reports were the same, compiled in the same way. They are of a scientific nature and can be verified. First of all, the day I visited, who was with me from my team, which of my staff was with me; for example, who was from the 3rd Brigade, a doctor from the 1st Brigade, that kind of thing. Then, afterwards, we would say what we found. And after that, and this is an important portion, we would propose measures as to what should be done, because we didn't have any type of command function, we're not part of the chain of command. All we can do is propose measures, because we have a consultative professional and educational/training body. After that, we would look at what would happen unless those measures were implemented. That would be in the conclusion. And then, finally, who these reports were addressed to. And the same thing was repeated for each and every case, each and every report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, would you take up the binder in front of you, and we'll go through the documents, through all the documents, looking at all the topics that you've been testifying about over this last hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. (redacted), there is one sentence where I do not quite understand what you want to say. It's page 46, line first. It says: "After that, after having examined, we would look at what would happen unless those measures were implemented." That's the sentence. I don't quite understand what you are saying here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what you should know is this: In preventive medicine, you forecast what a situation might be and you take steps to prevent adverse things from happening. Now, curative medicine, you treat persons straight away, where preventive medicine you make your forecast, you try and foresee what might happen and put measures in place to prevent infectious diseases from breaking out, specifically in my area. I think that's the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I understand that. The question that I would like to ask is whether you also verified and took note and reported on whether and how your recommendations were implemented.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. In some of the reports, it says on the basis of -- compared to my previous report, the situation is either better or worse, better because of such and such, worse because of such and such. So what we endeavour to do was to get a step-by-step advance and progress to prevent infectious diseases from breaking out. If you look at Heliodrom, infectious diseases know no boundaries. They will affect soldiers, their families, so they're contagious, they lead to the spread of disease.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you take a look at the first document now, please. It is P3355, which is a report on the work -- P3355 is the document number, and it is the report on the work of the Defence Department for January to June. Look at page 26 first, please. It relates to the Defence Department. I have a message telling me that Judge Trechsel, on page 46, line 11, mentioned the witness's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I apologise, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been corrected. The order has been filed. I'll probably have a cramp by the end of the afternoon if I continue this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best to prevent mistakes from happening, but of course anything can happen. Now we'd like to look at page 23 of the English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's 26 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's quite right. And here we have the Health Sector, which was the sector that included your own service; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at page 27 now, please. On page 27, which is page 24 of the English, we see that when the Health Sector, the Main Medical Corps HQ was active, now, is that the headquarters that your service was active in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now take a look at page 31, and in the English it is page 29. Have you found it? This is an epidemiological/toxicological report, or, rather, a report of the Infectious Diseases, Epidemiological and Toxicological Service. Witness, we don't have much time, but, anyway, over the next two pages of this report, we have a listing of all of your jobs -- all the tasks that you performed during the reporting period, where the final conclusion, the penultimate paragraph on page 33, which states that you compiled 81 daily reports and 21 weekly reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd just like to draw your attention to something we did not discuss yet. On page 32, it says that you compiled a series of instructions, sets of instructions, or, rather, your service, or you yourself, which applied, well, during this period of time in -- for the purpose of education, and you handed it over to the brigade's medical corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is just a part of it. There was much more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a general overview of your work, Witness, so you can skip the next document in the binder and find document 2D 2021. We're now moving on to what did you in concrete terms, 2021. It should be the third document in your binder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you help me, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, you mustn't display this document, because one might identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, then I think it would be a good idea to move into private session, and I'll do that for all the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we are in closed session, or public session, are we? Yes, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think it's -- excuse me, Your Honour. I don't think it's particularly critical. I won't -- out of an abundance of caution, I won't mention the name of the next witness, Your Honour. But just for scheduling purposes, it would assist the Prosecution, and presumably everyone else in the courtroom, if we knew what the schedule would be for the next witness and whether the witness will then start tomorrow or whether we'll be starting on the next witness on Wednesday, and I thought the Chamber might inquire. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. Nozica, what about the second witness this week? Is he going to be ready to testify tomorrow already or is it going to be Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to our schedule, the witness will be coming in on Wednesday, and he'll be ready for Wednesday because he's just arrived today, so we won't have another witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we should finish this witness tomorrow. Very well. At any rate, the Trial Chamber is going to issue a decision regarding the next witness, but it will be filed tomorrow or at least as soon as possible. I'm now addressing the Defence counsel who wish to cross-examine this witness. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to our internal order, I'm next for the cross-examination of this witness. I don't know whether you want me to start straight away or to hear the views about the other Defence teams, whether they will be cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it might be good to know who wants to cross-examine, to arrange time much. Are you going to speak, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. The Defence of General Praljak has no questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for Mr. Coric? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We're not sure yet, but even if we do have questions, it will just be one or two, briefly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For Mr. Pusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As things now stand, Mr. President, we probably don't have any questions for this witness, but we'll leave the decision to when our time comes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Dr. Prlic has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to officially wish everybody good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, too, Witness. My name is Vesna Alaburic, I'm an attorney from Zagreb, and in this trial I am Defence counsel for General Milivoj Petkovic. I'd like to you explain some of your answers, the answers you gave to the following questions: First of all, your supervision over the Heliodrom location; the second group of questions will relate to authorisation for taking decisions from the Health Sector of the Defence Department; and the third group of questions will relate to the establishment and organisation of the Health Sector and authorisations for appointments and dismissals so that we can see what the chain of command was like, the line of subordination. I'd like to ask the interpreters that if I do not use the chain of command, but the line of subordination, to use the same term in English, "chain of subordination," could "the chain of subordination" be used in the future. Thank you. So, Witness, about Heliodrom, if I notice correctly, the Defence of Bruno Stojic put three of your reports to you about a supervision over Heliodrom, and I'm interested in comparing two of them. The first document, and I'm sure you'll remember it, the first document is 2D 754, which is a report dated the 20th of July, 1993, and the second report is number P 5503, dated the 30th of September, 1993. If I analyse these reports correctly, Witness, in the first of those report mention is made of your communication with the Sanitary Service of the 3rd Brigade. And at the of September, in the report, the infirmary is mentioned of the Centre for Preventive Isolation, Heliodrom. Do you remember these differences, or would you like to look at the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you said, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the first document, dated the 20th of July, 1993, you mention your communication with the Sanitary Service of the 3rd Brigade, among other things, and in the second report, dated the 30th of September, under item 5, the infirmary of the centre is mentioned. Yes, the infirmary of the centre is mentioned, and it is the Centre for Preventive Isolation for Heliodrom. And I note that in September, you in fact contacted some other doctors and medical officers and not the staff of the 3rd Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the first point is this: The infirmary was set up -- and we're talking about the detainees; is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the persistent insistence, well, by me and my superior, the infirmary was set up. We -- the two of us kept insisting on that. We found doctors that we engaged, and once again when we persistently insisted, a stay -- an infirmary was set up. So we wanted to give a more qualitative form of professional assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at a document, and then you can tell me whether that is the decision, and could we provide the witness with that -- the set of documents and the two documents, two extra documents. Witness, you have two separate documents which we prepared. It is P 4145. It is a request by Mr. Bagaric, dated the 12th of August, 1993, to the effect that a sanitary station be set up at Heliodrom. And now, in the penultimate paragraph, it says to release -- "The physicians of the 3rd Brigade shall be relieved of all duties at Heliodrom." Do you know of this request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally don't, but this is a mistake, because in all our reports so far, the observation made is that the medical service of a particular brigade, of a specific brigade, and if we're talking about Heliodrom, that it is duty-bound to provide all the medical services, and here we mean the prison. So this is a mistake. And if you look at all the other reports -- well, this is a document that is unknown to me. I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, tell us, please, do you mean to say that this request by Mr. Bagaric about the establishment of a medical service at Heliodrom was never implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you misunderstood me. I was quite decisive in my first three sentences. At the insistence of Dr. Bagaric and me, we managed to set up the infirmary. That was the first organ. Then we set up a centre, medical centre, which was in an infirmary with beds, and that was located at Heliodrom. We found doctors who had been held in detention, and their work was controlled by the Medical Corps of the 3rd Brigade.
